summary:
LunaScope: Making Lunar South-Pole Exploration More Informed

Exploring the Moon's south pole is one of the most challenging tasks in future lunar missions. Its rugged terrain, constantly changing sunlight, long periods of shadow, and limited visibility of Earth make mission planning extremely complex. A location that looks promising on a map may not provide the conditions needed for sustained surface operations.

LunaScope is an interactive lunar mission-planning and terrain analysis platform designed to help explore these challenges using real scientific data.** By combining NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data with NASA/JPL SPICE orbital geometry, LunaScope transforms complex lunar measurements into an accessible 3D exploration and analysis experience.

Users can explore measured lunar terrain, select locations and mission dates, visualize the calculated positions of the Sun and Earth, and examine how terrain affects sunlight and geometric Earth visibility. The platform also compares potential operating locations, identifies mission windows based on configurable constraints, and estimates solar-power generation and battery performance under user-defined engineering assumptions.
details:
LunaScope: An Intelligent Lunar South-Pole Terrain and Mission Planning Platform

1. The Problem We Are Addressing

The lunar south pole is an important region for future lunar exploration, but planning surface operations there is far from straightforward. Its landscape contains steep slopes, craters, elevated ridges, and areas that experience challenging lighting conditions. Sunlight can remain available for extended periods in some locations while disappearing behind terrain in others. At the same time, the ability to geometrically see Earth from a surface location can change throughout a mission.

These conditions create several connected questions for mission planners:

  • Which terrain locations offer more favourable operating conditions?
  • How will sunlight availability change during a planned mission?
  • Can surrounding terrain obstruct the Sun or Earth's apparent position?
  • When might an operation experience extended periods of darkness or limited Earth visibility?
  • How might these conditions affect an assumed solar-power and battery configuration?

LunaScope addresses these questions through one connected, interactive analysis environment.

2. Our Proposed Solution

LunaScope is an independent lunar surface exploration and mission-planning platform that brings together authentic lunar elevation data, astronomical calculations, 3D terrain visualization, and configurable mission analysis.

Instead of relying on a static lunar map or presenting isolated scientific measurements, the platform allows users to select a terrain location, choose a date and UTC time, explore the surrounding landscape, and investigate how the Sun and Earth appear from that particular position.

The system uses official NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) terrain data, combined with NASA/JPL SPICE ephemeris and lunar orientation kernels. These inputs are processed to calculate terrain horizons, Sun and Earth directions, visibility conditions, and potential operating windows.

Our goal is to make complex lunar mission-planning information easier to explore, compare, understand, and reproduce.

3. Key Features and Capabilities

A. Interactive 3D Lunar Terrain Exploration

LunaScope provides a rotatable 3D Moon globe and a detailed local terrain explorer. Users can move between the global lunar view and the selected surface region to understand both the broader geography and the local landscape.

The terrain explorer uses elevation measurements from the installed 80-metre-per-pixel LOLA south-polar dataset. Users can select locations directly on the terrain and inspect their coordinates and elevation.

The Sun's calculated position also influences the terrain visualization, helping users understand how lighting conditions change over time.

B. Sunlight and Earth Visibility Analysis

One of LunaScope's central capabilities is analysing how the surrounding terrain affects the visibility of the Sun and Earth.

The platform calculates their directions using NASA/JPL SPICE geometry and checks those directions against the local terrain horizon.

It distinguishes between different operating conditions, including:

  • Adequate solar-disk visibility with Earth-center clearance.
  • Adequate solar visibility when the Earth center is obstructed.
  • Limited solar visibility despite geometric Earth visibility.
  • Conditions where both are obstructed.

It also estimates the visible fraction of the solar and Earth disks. This provides more information than simply labelling a location as illuminated or shadowed.

C. Mission Planner and Location Comparison

The Mission Planner allows users to configure mission dates, UTC start times, operational duration, sunlight requirements, Earth-visibility requirements, and other constraints.

It evaluates the available analysis locations against these requirements and presents ranked results with explanations of failed conditions.

Users can compare up to three locations and select primary and backup options. The system does not silently recommend a location when the configured requirements are not satisfied.

The current project includes 13 reproducibly selected analysis points derived from actual lunar elevation-raster measurements. These are project analysis locations, not NASA-approved landing sites.

D. Mission Timeline and Operating Windows

A lunar mission is not defined by a single moment. Conditions can change significantly throughout an operation.

LunaScope therefore provides a timeline showing sunlight availability, geometric Earth visibility, combined operating states, and estimated battery charge along a shared mission-time cursor.

Its mission-window finder evaluates potential start times against configurable operational constraints. It considers factors such as minimum sunlight availability, maximum shadow duration, Earth-visibility requirements, and the requested operation duration.

The purpose is to help users investigate more favourable periods for carrying out planned surface operations.

E. Solar Power and Battery Estimation

Environmental conditions also influence the power available to a lunar surface system.

LunaScope includes a configurable electrical model that estimates solar-panel generation, electrical load, battery charging and discharging, remaining battery charge, and potential unmet power demand.

Users can adjust assumptions such as:

  • Solar-panel area and efficiency.
  • Panel orientation and derating.
  • Electrical power consumption.
  • Battery capacity and initial charge.
  • Charging and discharging efficiency.
  • Required battery reserve.

This connects environmental analysis with an important engineering consideration: whether an assumed power system can support the planned operation under the calculated illumination conditions.

F. Educational and Scientific Transparency

LunaScope also includes an Educator Mode that explains terrain clearance, sunlight, and geometric Earth visibility through accessible diagrams and visual demonstrations.

Its Data & Sources section makes the scientific inputs, processing methods, and data provenance visible to users.

We consider transparency an essential part of the project. When a required scientific input is missing, the platform reports the result as unavailable instead of replacing it with fabricated measurements.

4. Scientific Data and Technology

The project uses real scientific datasets and established computational tools.

Primary scientific sources:

  • NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO).
  • Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) south-polar elevation data.
  • NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE planetary ephemeris and lunar orientation kernels.
  • JPL Horizons for independent comparisons of selected Sun and Earth direction calculations.

Technology stack:

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D Visualization: Three.js.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Scientific Computation: NumPy, SciPy and SpiceyPy.
  • Terrain Processing: Rasterio and Pillow.
  • Communication: REST APIs and WebSockets.
  • Testing: Pytest and browser-based Playwright checks.
  • Deployment: Docker with deployment configurations for cloud hosting.

5. What Makes LunaScope Different?

LunaScope brings several connected layers of lunar analysis into one platform.

Rather than treating terrain visualization, sunlight calculations, Earth visibility, mission scheduling, and power estimation as separate problems, it connects them through shared locations, UTC settings, and mission configurations.

Another important aspect is its focus on explainability. Users can inspect why a location satisfies or fails a particular constraint instead of receiving an unexplained recommendation.

The project also maintains a clear distinction between published scientific measurements, calculated results, engineering assumptions, and illustrative visualizations.

This means users can explore the outputs while understanding what the system actually knows, what it estimates, and where information remains unavailable.

6. Testing and Validation

We have placed significant emphasis on verifying the implementation rather than relying only on visual demonstrations.

Recorded project verification includes:

  • 64 passing backend automated tests following the exact-pole correction.
  • Integrity and SHA-256 checks for all seven installed scientific input files.
  • Verification of all 13 catalog elevations against the original LOLA raster pixels.
  • 12 selected Sun and Earth direction comparisons against independent JPL Horizons results, passing the chosen 0.02-degree tolerance.
  • Successful frontend production build and strict TypeScript checks.
  • Browser testing of terrain exploration, location selection, timeline controls, comparisons, power settings, exports, and mission-window tools.
  • Mobile layout checks across all six application routes at a 390 × 844 viewport.
  • Successful production-container build and recorded Linux smoke tests.

These results demonstrate substantial implementation and software verification work. They are not a claim of flight qualification or certified lunar landing safety.

7. Expected Impact and Future Potential

We see LunaScope as a way to make lunar surface analysis more accessible to students, researchers, and people interested in future space exploration.

It provides a practical environment for investigating how terrain, illumination, Earth visibility, mission timing, and power assumptions interact.

The platform can also serve as a foundation for future development, including integration of higher-resolution lunar terrain products, improved terrain uncertainty information, more detailed surface-hazard analysis, and additional mission-planning capabilities.

Our broader vision is to support more informed exploration of the lunar south pole by turning scientific datasets into an interactive environment where users can ask meaningful questions and investigate the results themselves.

8. Our Vision

We believe that planning a lunar mission should involve more than identifying a location on a map. It requires understanding the terrain, the changing environment, and the conditions under which a mission may need to operate.

LunaScope brings these elements together in a single scientific exploration platform.

Understand the terrain. Explore the conditions. Plan the mission.

LunaScope aims to make the complex environment of the lunar south pole easier to investigate, one location and one mission window at a time.
